The Early Cretaceous pterosaur Pterodaustro guinazui exhibits a unique filter-feeding ecology that has drawn considerable attention from paleobiologists studying the origins of edentulous feeding in pterosaurs. Hatchlings of this species emerge from eggs with a skull length at birth of only 3 centimeters [Lb = 3 centimeters], a remarkably small dimension given the eventual size of the cranium. The preserved egg from which this estimate derives suggests that the neonates were highly altricial, requiring intensive parental care during the initial weeks post-hatching. The overall skull length of an adult individual reaches approximately 29 centimeters [Li = approximately 29 centimeters], indicating a nearly tenfold increase in cranial size from hatching to maturity. This dramatic elongation of the rostrum is accompanied by the development of hundreds of long, thin teeth specialized for straining small aquatic prey from sediment-rich water. The growth trajectory of the skull in Pterodaustro thus reflects a profound dietary shift from a presumably insectivorous or particle-feeding juvenile niche to the specialized filter-feeding apparatus of the fully grown animal, a transition that would have required substantial metabolic investment over the course of development.

Reproductive output in Pterodaustro guinazui remains poorly constrained due to the rarity of nesting sites, but speculative estimates have been derived from comparisons with modern flamingos and other filter-feeding altricial birds, which occupy a similar ecological niche. Under stable thermal conditions of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the maximum reproductive rate has been proposed to be extraordinarily low, equivalent to approximately 10 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 10 offspring per year] when considering a single clutch annually. This figure is based on the limited available nesting material from the Lagarcito Formation, where egg clutches typically contain two or three eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two or three eggs per clutch], and evidence suggests that females produce only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year]. Such a low annual fecundity is consistent with the life-history strategy of a long-lived, slow-maturing vertebrate that invests heavily in the survival of each offspring. Although highly speculative, these estimates provide a valuable baseline for comparative analyses with other pterosaurs and extant archosaurs that share similar constraints on reproductive investment.

Body mass at hatching for this species has been calculated from egg dimensions preserved in the fossil record, revealing that a hatchling Pterodaustro guinazui emerges with an initial wet weight of approximately 30 grams [Ww0 = approximately 30 grams]. This value was derived from the length and width of a well-preserved egg, which indicate a spherical volume consistent with an altricial developmental mode. In stark contrast, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is estimated to be around 4500 grams [Wwi = around 4500 grams], representing a substantial increase in body mass over the course of ontogeny. This asymptotic mass places Pterodaustro among the larger-bodied pterosaurs, though it remains considerably smaller than the giant azhdarchids of the Late Cretaceous. The rapid growth required to achieve this adult mass within a relatively short period would have necessitated an abundant and predictable food supply, reinforcing the interpretation that these animals inhabited productive lacustrine or coastal environments where filter-feeding could be sustained year-round.

Longevity estimates for Pterodaustro guinazui, derived from growth line counts in long bones and comparisons with modern birds, suggest that these animals were capable of living for extended periods. When maintaining an active body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], comparable to that of modern endothermic birds, the maximum lifespan is estimated to be approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years]. This duration is remarkably long for a pterosaur of this body size and is consistent with a life-history strategy characterized by delayed reproduction, low annual fecundity, and high parental investment in each offspring. The presence of multiple growth rings in histological sections of limb bones supports the interpretation that individuals experienced seasonal fluctuations in resource availability, which would have influenced growth rates and potentially contributed to the observed longevity. The ability to buffer extended periods of food scarcity through stored energy reserves would have been critical for survival during the harsh Cretaceous winters of southern South America.

Puberty in Pterodaustro guinazui, defined as the onset of gonadal activity and the ability to reproduce, is estimated to occur after an extended period of somatic growth. Under the same thermoregulatory regime of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], the time since birth at puberty is estimated at approximately 730 days [tp = approximately 730 days], equivalent to roughly two years of age. This delayed maturation is consistent with the pattern observed in many long-lived, low-fecundity vertebrates, particularly those that invest heavily in the physical development of a specialized feeding apparatus. The prolonged juvenile period would have allowed individuals to acquire the full complement of filter-feeding teeth and the elongated rostrum needed to exploit adult prey resources efficiently. Comparative analyses with modern Crocodylia and large altricial birds suggest that such a delay in reproductive maturity serves to maximize somatic growth, reduce adult mortality associated with reproduction, and ultimately increase lifetime fitness in an environment where competition for food resources was intense.
